title: WebAnything: From the Wild Web to Scalable Agent Environments
summary:
arXiv:2610.37786v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Web agents require diverse, executable, and resettable website environments for reproducible training and evaluation. Human-assisted mirrors demand per-site engineering, while generative construction can diverge from specified real websites. Capture-and-replay preserves observations, with interaction coverage constrained by captured content and replay capabilities.
  We present WebAnything, a fully automated framework that reconstructs source-grounded, reusable Web environments from real URLs without per-site manual implementation or repair after initial setup and authorization. An Explorer-Builder collects browser-observable structures, resources, and interaction outcomes; an independent verifier checks frozen candidates and guides local repair or targeted source recapture.
  We construct 244 website artifacts across 14 application domains and 53 categories, supporting 12,984 executed and accepted tasks. Compared with human-assisted WebHarbor, WebAnything achieves higher aggregate scores on three fidelity metrics, with 12 wins, two ties, and no losses in a blind audit. Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B on 5,856 interaction trajectories improves REAL success by 9.9 percentage points, Odysseys-Easy Rubric Avg and Task Avg by 6.25 and 6.32 percentage points, and WebArena-Verified Overall success by 13.33 percentage points under the fixed harness. Code: https://github.com/china-qijizhifeng/Web-Anything

title: Multi-Token Prediction Done Right [R]
summary: Sharing one of our latest papers on Multi-Token Prediction (MTP). MTP is now a standard recipe for frontier pre-training but turns out, it can be done much better.We show the standard MTP gradient hides a KL self-distillation signal (which we want for improving speculative decoding) behind a noisy residual (that harms next-token prediction).I think the coolest part was the KL gradient–recovery trick to extract the KL gradient. You just need a one-line code change:h_ntp += h_mtp.detach() - h_mtpSoft Multi-Token Prediction (Soft-MTP)is essentially a free lunch that improves MTP across a range of tasks.I'm super excited about this work. title: I built a scikit-learn for RSI [P]
summary: After reading a bunch of RSI papers, I keep coming back to familiar problems from RL and evolutionary search:Sampling:How do we find promising changes efficiently?Evaluation:How do we know a new variant actually improves the agent?Diversity:How do we avoid converging too early?That motivated us to buildGear, an open-source, meta-learning-inspired framework. A task agent produces execution traces; a meta-agent uses those traces and evaluation feedback to improve prompts, tools, workflows, and context management.Gear separates search decisions from execution and evaluation. Our goal is ascikit-learn for RSI, making approaches such as GEPA, RRSI, and Harness² easier to implement and compare. We currently have a working GEPA variant with shared failure diagnosis and staged evaluation.WithGPT 5.6 Luna held at medium reasoning effort, we observed these task pass rates:BenchmarkBase DSHGear-optimized DSHAutomationBench Marketing27.0%40.0%AutomationBench Support17.0%25.0%Terminal-Bench 2.152.8%62.9%At max effort on Marketing, Luna with the optimized harness reached88.88% objective completion, versus84.08% for Astra + Codex. Strict task pass rates were53% versus 57%, so the advantage was in partial completion.Separately, with both models using thesame optimized DSH at max effort, Luna’s estimated API cost averaged$0.0568 per task versus $1.1858 for Astra—95.21% lower, excluding optimization and infrastructure costs.We’d welcome feedback on candidate evaluation and diversity preservation under limited budgets.Code·Papersubmitted by/u/Pale-Training-6944[link][comments]

title: obra /superpowers
summary: Superpowers Superpowers is a complete software development methodology for your coding agents, built on top of a set of composable skills and some initial instructions that make sure your agent uses them. Table of Contents How it works Commercial Services Getting Started Claude Code Antigravity Codex App Codex CLI Cursor Devin CLI Factory Droid Gemini CLI GitHub Copilot CLI Grok Build CLI Kimi Code OpenCode Pi Qwen Code Hermes Agent Muse The Basic Workflow When Something Goes Wrong Community What's Inside Philosophy Contributing Updating License Visual companion telemetry How it works It starts from the moment you fire up your coding agent. As soon as it sees that you're building something, it doesn't just jump into trying to write code. Instead, it steps back and asks you what you're really trying to do. Once it's teased a spec out of the conversation, it shows it to you in chunks short enough to actually read and digest. After you've signed off on the design, your agent puts together an implementation plan that's clear enough for an enthusiastic junior engineer with poor taste, no judgement, no project context, and an aversion to testing to follow. It emphasizes true red/green TDD, YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It), and DRY. Next up, once you say "go", it launches a subagent-driven-development process, having agents work through each engineering task, inspecting and reviewing their work, and continuing forward. It's not uncommon for your agent to work autonomously for a couple hours at a time without deviating from the plan you put together. There's a bunch more to it, but that's the core of the system. And because the skills trigger automatically, you don't need to do anything special. Your coding agent just has Superpowers. title: Donchitos /Claude-Code-Game-Studios
summary: Claude Code Game Studios Turn a single Claude Code session into a full game development studio. 49 agents. 74 skills. One coordinated AI team. Why This Exists Building a game solo with AI is powerful — but a single chat session has no structure. No one stops you from hardcoding magic numbers, skipping design docs, or writing spaghetti code. There's no QA pass, no design review, no one asking "does this actually fit the game's vision?" Claude Code Game Studios solves this by giving your AI session the structure of a real studio. Instead of one general-purpose assistant, you get 49 specialized agents organized into a studio hierarchy — directors who guard the vision, department leads who own their domains, and specialists who do the hands-on work. Each agent has defined responsibilities, escalation paths, and quality gates. The result: you still make every decision, but now you have a team that asks the right questions, catches mistakes early, and keeps your project organized from first brainstorm to launch. summary: Mark Zuckerberg's Meta made AI look so stinking cute by giving it a squishy little face - and this holiday season, he wants to sell you a Muse Charm so you can carry your jolly AI helper around like a Tamagotchi. But I won't be buying one, because we have Muse Charm at home. It […]
title_es: DIY: construir un Tamagotchi IA antes que Meta Muse
bajada: Un desarrollador construyó su propio Tamagotchi IA antes del lanzamiento oficial de Meta Muse Charm, demostrando que la tecnología es accesible para builders independientes. El proyecto muestra cómo desarrolladores pueden replicar productos de grandes empresas con herramientas abiertas.
bajada_en: A developer built a DIY AI Tamagotchi before Meta's official Muse Charm launch, showing the technology is accessible to independent builders. The project demonstrates how developers can replicate corporate products with open tools.
